topThree.teaser: Treasury fintech Embat partners with J.P. Morgan to enable direct bank account connectivity for corporate clients.
topThree.whatItIs: An integration of J.P. Morgan’s banking authorization service (BAS) API into Embat’s treasury management platform.
topThree.whyItMatters: Streamlines bank-treasury connectivity, allowing joint clients to manage J.P. Morgan accounts directly within Embat’s interface.
topThree.bankAngle: Demonstrates how banks can leverage APIs to embed their services into third-party treasury management platforms.
topThree.imageAlt: Embat integrates J.P. Morgan banking authorization service API

topThree.longSummary:
## The story

Embat, a fintech that builds treasury management software, has integrated J.P. Morgan’s banking authorization service (BAS) API into its platform. The partnership was announced on November 4 via a press release provided to PYMNTS. By connecting the two systems, joint clients can link their J.P. Morgan bank accounts directly to Embat’s treasury interface without first obtaining certificates from an external certification authority. Embat explains that the traditional certification process typically requires extensive implementation, data validation and signatures, often stretching over months before a client can begin operations. With the new integration, clients can authenticate and connect their accounts in seconds, and no IT development is required. The company also notes that it is the first treasury management system to leverage J.P. Morgan’s own user interface through the API, allowing the bank’s branding and workflow to appear within Embat’s environment.

The integration is designed to streamline client account activation and reduce operational effort for treasury teams. It is especially useful for organizations that operate multiple subsidiaries or legal entities, because they no longer need to repeat the bank‑connection process for each entity. Instead, a single multi‑tenant certificate provided by J.P. Morgan covers all subsidiaries, enabling finance teams to onboard and manage every corporate entity from one console. Antonio Berga, Embat’s co‑founder and co‑CEO, said the partnership eliminates “time‑consum ing and tedious” bank connectivity processes, cutting the time needed from months to days without any technical development. The move is expected to accelerate adoption among mid‑sized firms that previously found the certification barrier prohibitive.

## Key details

The BAS API provides a single multi‑tenant certificate that secures connections for multiple subsidiaries under one security setup. According to Embat, clients only need to sign legal documentation that authorizes the platform to access their accounts; once that is done, the connection becomes active. The integration is built for companies with several legal entities, as it removes the requirement to repeat the bank‑connection procedure for each subsidiary. Embat’s platform includes AI‑driven analytics, and the company says the combination of real‑time data and the bank’s security enables faster, more informed decision making. The multi‑tenant certificate also simplifies compliance with the bank's security policies, as all subsidiaries are covered under a single credential.

PYMNTS reported in late September that the treasury‑management market is shifting from simply aggregating information to executing actions based on those signals. The article noted that software has spent years collecting data from bank portals, spreadsheets and enterprise systems, and the next generation is expected to interpret those signals. In a separate survey by PYMNTS Intelligence, 15.7% of small‑ to medium‑sized businesses cited better card and spending analytics as a factor in choosing a primary corporate card, while 13.8% mentioned improved expense management. These figures illustrate the demand for tools that not only present data but also support operational decisions.

## Why it matters

The partnership addresses a long‑standing friction point in corporate treasury: the manual, certificate‑heavy process of linking a bank to a software platform. By embedding J.P. Morgan’s authorization service, Embat offers a smoother onboarding experience that can shorten implementation timelines and reduce operational overhead. For banks, the move illustrates a strategy to embed their services directly into third‑party platforms, preserving customer relationships while expanding their reach. For treasury teams, the ability to manage multiple entities from a single interface may improve visibility and control over cash positions. The integration also signals a broader trend of banks opening their APIs to fintech partners, which could accelerate innovation in cash management and payment services.

The shift toward execution‑oriented treasury tools, as described by PYMNTS, suggests that platforms which combine data aggregation with automated action are becoming the norm. As more firms adopt such integrated solutions, the competitive landscape may reward providers that can deliver seamless, secure connectivity alongside advanced analytics. This development could prompt other banks to develop comparable API‑based connectivity options, further intensifying competition in the treasury technology space.

topThree.teaser: Revolut becomes New Zealand's 27th registered bank, marking its official entry as the country's first digital bank.
topThree.whatItIs: A digital banking platform officially registered as a bank by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.
topThree.whyItMatters: Expands Revolut's global footprint and introduces digital-only banking competition to the New Zealand market.
topThree.bankAngle: Highlights the ongoing global expansion of digital-first banking models and regulatory licensing.
topThree.imageAlt: Revolut launches as a registered bank in New Zealand

signalScore.rationale: Significant market entry for a major global digital bank.

topThree.longSummary:
## Story
Revolut officially launched in New Zealand as a registered bank after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand registered Revolut Bank New Zealand Limited. The registration makes Revolut the country’s 27th registered bank and its first digital bank. The milestone follows Revolut’s initial entry into the New Zealand market in 2023, when it operated as a financial services provider before securing full bank status. Along with the bank registration, Revolut announced Instant Access Savings accounts with eligible deposits up to NZ$100,000 protected by the New Zealand Depositor Compensation Scheme. The accounts carry a 3.50 percent variable introductory savings rate for an initial four-month period. Revolut committed to investing NZ$120 million into the local market over the next five years. The company aims to enhance the financial wellbeing of New Zealand residents and bring competition to a sector long dominated by traditional players. Revolut Founder and CEO Nik Storonsky said the launch marks another step toward building the world’s first truly global bank and that securing a seventh bank license and fifth this year reflects the strength of the company’s business model. Revolut Bank New Zealand CEO Ryan Brosnahan said becoming a bank in New Zealand is a defining moment achieved through a focus on delivering a better financial experience for Kiwis, noting the market is primed for disruption. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s registration also subjects Revolut to local prudential standards, aligning the entity with New Zealand’s banking regulatory framework. The registration extends Revolut’s licensing presence into the Pacific region, complementing its existing operations in Europe and Oceania.

## Key details
Revolut now holds seven banking licenses and operates as a licensed bank in 34 geographies, including the United Kingdom, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand. The company’s global customer base exceeds 80 million. In addition to the New Zealand registration, Revolut recently secured new licenses and authorizations in the United Arab Emirates, Mexico, Colombia, and Peru. The company has advanced its United States bank charter application with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and received approval to acquire Banco Cetelem in Argentina. In 2015, Revolut CEO Nik Storonsky demonstrated the company’s banking platform at FinovateEurope in London. Revolut’s entry into New Zealand broadens its reach as a global banking competitor. While other international digital banks such as Brazil-based Nubank have largely focused expansion on specific regions, Revolut is pursuing a more geographically diverse strategy. The company’s approach positions it to compete directly with traditional financial institutions rather than simply offering an alternative digital financial services platform. The New Zealand registration follows Revolut’s launch in the country in 2023 as a financial services provider. Instant Access Savings accounts are subject to the New Zealand Depositor Compensation Scheme, which protects eligible deposits up to NZ$100,000. The 3.50 percent variable introductory rate applies for four months.

## Why it matters
Revolut’s launch as a registered bank in New Zealand introduces digital-only competition into a market where traditional institutions have long held sway. The company’s commitment of NZ$120 million over five years signals a sustained investment in the region. By securing a banking license, Revolut gains the ability to offer deposit products protected under New Zealand’s scheme, expanding its service model beyond transactional finance. The move also underscores a broader trend of fintech firms seeking full bank charters to compete on equal footing with incumbents. Revolut’s geographically diverse licensing strategy, spanning Europe, Oceania, the Middle East, Latin America, and North America, contrasts with rivals that concentrate on fewer regions. For the New Zealand banking sector, the entry of a global digital player with over 80 million customers worldwide may increase pressure on incumbents to innovate on cost, speed, and user experience. The registration also reflects the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s regulatory framework allowing foreign digital banks to operate under local protection schemes. Observers will likely watch how quickly Revolut scales its New Zealand user base and whether the introductory savings rate translates into sustained customer acquisition beyond the promotional period.

## The story
Nuvei has secured a license for local payment acceptance in South Africa, according to Payments Afrika. The authorization advances the company’s Every Payment Everywhere strategy, extending its presence within domestic payment ecosystems to help businesses optimize payment performance in every market they operate. The company adds South Africa to its network and says it is extending its local acquiring and payment acceptance infrastructure, transaction data, and operational controls to another major market, accessible through a single global platform.

The authorization is described as allowing Nuvei to support global brands and local businesses with localized payment processing capabilities. Phil Fayer, Chair and CEO of Nuvei, said, “Commerce is global, but payment performance is local.” He said the expansion into South Africa is another step toward giving businesses access to locally optimized payment capabilities at global scale. The company said South Africa is one of Africa’s most important digital commerce markets, and that strengthening its presence there creates new opportunities for international businesses entering the region and South African companies expanding globally.

## Key details
According to the article, South Africa’s B2C ecommerce market grew by an estimated 9.9% in 2025 to reach $8.48 billion, based on research published by PayNXT360. The market was forecast to expand at a compound annual growth rate of 8.3% through 2029, reaching approximately $11.66 billion. The article said this continued growth is increasing the importance of locally optimized payment performance for businesses competing in the market.

Nuvei’s approach, as described, is to add South Africa to its network. The company said this extends local acquiring and payment acceptance infrastructure, transaction data, and operational controls to another major market, accessible through a single global platform. The article then explains that processing transactions domestically can improve authorization rates compared with cross-border acquiring, reduce processing costs, and give businesses more complete visibility into transaction performance. It also said direct access to local transaction data supports more precise fraud management and enables businesses to identify and address sources of payment friction more effectively.

For global brands entering South Africa, the article said they will be able to access these capabilities through the same Nuvei integration they use across other markets. Businesses already serving South African consumers cross-border will be able to establish a more locally optimized payments operation without adding a separate gateway, acquiring relationship, and reporting environment. The article added that this gives them room to adapt the checkout experience to local expectations while managing authorization, fraud prevention, reconciliation, and reporting through one platform.

## Why it matters
The Nuvei news matters to anyone following payment infrastructure because it shows how a global fintech can seek to localize its operations market by market. The South Africa license is not only a regulatory step for Nuvei; it is also positioned as part of a commercial strategy to help businesses improve payment performance. The reported growth in South Africa’s ecommerce market adds context, even though the figures are estimates and forecasts.

The article’s claims about domestic processing are central. Compared with cross-border acquiring, domestic processing may improve authorization rates, reduce costs, and provide more visibility. Better access to local transaction data may also support fraud management. For global brands, this could lower barriers to entering South Africa. For local businesses, the effect may depend on how Nuvei’s platform is used and how banks and regulators view the arrangements.

For a bank or product team, the briefing note may be relevant because payment acceptance, fraud, reconciliation, and reporting are often fragmented across providers and financial institutions. Nuvei’s pitch is that a single global platform can handle these functions for cross-border and local operations. The South Africa authorization is a step toward that capability being more fully available in a major market.

The strategic implication is that Nuvei is using local licenses and infrastructure to support a global platform strategy. The Every Payment Everywhere strategy is described as extending domestic payment ecosystem presence to help businesses optimize payment performance. South Africa is presented as another important market. The company’s leadership framed the move as giving businesses access to locally optimized capabilities at global scale.

Overall, the story is about Nuvei securing local payment acceptance authority in South Africa and connecting it to its broader expansion plans. The key details include the license, the reported ecommerce market size and forecast, and the potential operational benefits of local processing. The importance lies in the market opportunity and the competitive positioning for payment infrastructure providers. The article does not provide a full assessment of implementation, regulation, or bank partnerships, so those questions remain open.

fintech.longSummary:
## Story
Settle, an inventory financing fintech founded in 2019, has entered a forward-flow financing agreement with 3Jane, a crypto-native structured credit platform, to expand its small and medium enterprise lending capacity. The deal, initially providing $50 million with an option to grow to $100 million, allows Settle to sell eligible loans to 3Jane on an ongoing basis. This structure frees capital for new loan originations rather than holding loans on its balance sheet until maturity. The agreement leverages stablecoin liquidity to finance real-world lending to consumer brands and ecommerce businesses. It follows Settle’s prior securing of a $240 million credit facility from an international financial institution and a New York-based asset manager, as well as a $280 million revolving credit facility in 2022 and a $145 million facility in 2023. As part of the arrangement, 3Jane has already purchased $18 million of Settle’s existing loans and committed to buying eligible new loans going forward. Settle’s CEO Alek Koenig emphasized the importance of helping consumer brands finance inventory purchases before generating revenue from sales, stating the forward flow provides a more capital-efficient way to finance that gap at scale. 3Jane CEO Jacob Chudnovsky highlighted the role of stablecoin liquidity in supporting Settle’s lending operations, noting that the financing structure is designed to lower Settle’s borrowing costs. The transaction marks a concrete example of digital asset capital being deployed into traditional SME lending products.

## Key Details
The financing agreement is structured as a forward-flow arrangement, under which Settle originates inventory financing loans–typically used by consumer brands and ecommerce businesses to pay suppliers upfront and repaid through extended payment terms or scheduled installments–and sells them to 3Jane on an ongoing basis. 3Jane operates a revolving conduit powered by blockchain technology, using stablecoin liquidity to provide capital to fintech lenders. The initial $50 million capacity can be expanded to $100 million, subject to eligibility and ongoing purchases. Beyond this agreement, Settle has established a track record of large credit facilities: $240 million announced last month, a $280 million revolving facility in 2022, and a $145 million facility in 2023. Since its founding in 2019, Settle has provided more than $4 billion in funding to thousands of consumer brands and ecommerce businesses. In addition to lending, the company offers a suite of cash flow management tools, including bill pay, accounts payable automation, and invoice tracking. The $18 million of existing loans already purchased by 3Jane represents the first tranche under the forward-flow agreement, demonstrating immediate engagement between the two platforms.

## Why It Matters
The deal highlights the growing connection between traditional lending and blockchain-based finance, as stablecoin liquidity is used to fund real-world loans to consumer brands. For Settle, the forward-flow structure improves capital efficiency by recycling capital into new originations rather than holding loans to maturity, supporting faster scaling of lending operations. The partnership also provides 3Jane with a channel to deploy digital asset capital into institutional-grade credit, diversifying its use cases beyond speculative markets. As stablecoin markets mature and regulatory frameworks evolve, such collaborations may become a more common pathway for fintechs to access liquidity and expand financing for small businesses. The transaction underscores a broader trend of crypto-native structured credit platforms partnering with fintech lenders to bridge digital asset capital with Main Street credit demand, potentially reshaping the SME financing landscape.

ai_software.headline: Anthropic develops FlashProve to verify AI model identity
ai_software.teaser: Anthropic is working on a system to prove the origin of AI responses.
ai_software.whatItIs: A system called FlashProve that allows users to verify an AI response's source.
ai_software.whyItMatters: Addresses concerns regarding AI authenticity and trust in generated content.
ai_software.bankAngle: Critical for banks using AI to ensure the integrity of automated customer interactions.
ai_software.imageAlt: Anthropic develops FlashProve to verify AI model identity

signalScore.rationale: Addresses AI trust issues relevant to financial services.

ai_software.longSummary:
## The story  
Anthropic announced an open‑source research project called **FlashProve** that aims to let users cryptographically verify which AI model generated a particular output. The system provides “provable inference,” a mathematical guarantee that a given response truly originated from the claimed model. The announcement was posted on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and published by TechCrunch’s AI editor Russell Brandom.  

FlashProve works by having AI labs publish a **fingerprint** for each released model. This fingerprint can later be matched to specific outputs and verified without revealing the model’s internal weights—information that companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. The approach is designed to be lightweight, allowing verification on a local device. Researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code on GitHub under an open‑source license, inviting the broader community to review, adapt, and improve the system.  

The project is still in an intermediate research phase; Anthropic has no immediate plans to deploy FlashProve commercially. The goal is to share early results and encourage further development by other labs and organizations interested in trustworthy AI outputs.  

## Key details  
- **Name and type**: FlashProve, an open‑source system for provable inference.  
- **Core mechanism**: Cryptographic fingerprints that link model outputs to specific AI models without exposing model weights.  
- **Verification method**: Lightweight checks that can be performed on a local device, similar to cryptographic email signatures.  
- **Publication**: Technical specification and code released on GitHub under an open‑source license.  
- **Timeline**: Announced on November 3, 2026; described as “intermediate progress” with ongoing research.  
- **Deployment status**: No plans to roll out FlashProve at Anthropic or any other lab at this time.  
- **Intended uses**: Preventing secret model swaps (e.g., cheaper or more powerful models), enabling third‑party verification of AI‑driven claims, and supporting transparency in AI‑generated content.  
- **Source**: Blog post referenced in TechCrunch article by Russell Brandom.  

## Why it matters  
The rise of large language models and other generative AI systems has heightened concerns about the authenticity of AI‑produced content. Users often cannot tell whether a response comes from the model they expect, which can lead to misinformation, unfair competition, or hidden cost‑cutting practices by AI providers.  

FlashProve addresses this trust gap by offering a cryptographic method to confirm model identity, akin to how digital signatures verify email senders. By allowing independent verification without exposing proprietary model weights, the system could become a standard tool for:  

1. **Transparency and accountability** – Companies can demonstrate that they are using the model they claim, which is valuable for regulatory compliance and consumer confidence.  
2. **Fair benchmarking** – Researchers and evaluators can be confident that performance numbers reflect the intended model, not a hidden substitute.  
3. **Third‑party verification** – Legal, financial, or security professionals could verify that critical tasks (e.g., vulnerability scanning or business‑plan review) were performed by a model meeting required standards.  

The open‑source nature of FlashProve also encourages collaboration across the AI community, reducing the risk of a single vendor’s proprietary solution becoming a de‑facto standard. By releasing the technology early, Anthropic aims to gather feedback and foster improvements that could benefit the broader ecosystem.  

While the system is not yet ready for production use, its development signals a growing focus on provenance and trust in AI outputs. As AI adoption expands into high‑stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, tools that can reliably attribute generated content to its source will become increasingly important for safety, compliance, and user confidence.

health_bio.headline: Leipzig-based JawBuddy raises €818k for jaw pain relief
health_bio.teaser: HealthTech startup JawBuddy secures pre-Seed funding to address TMJ and bruxism.
health_bio.whatItIs: A health technology solution for reducing jaw pain and tension.
health_bio.whyItMatters: Provides a specialized digital health tool for common dental and muscular issues.
health_bio.imageAlt: Leipzig-based JawBuddy raises €818k for jaw pain relief
health_bio.longSummary:
## The story

Leipzig-based health technology startup JawBuddy has closed a €818,000 pre-seed financing round led by healthcare investment platform HALBZEIT. The round also included participation from dental specialists Dr. Siegfried Marquardt and Dr. Guido Sigron, regional investor Mittelständische Beteiligungsgesellschaft Sachsen (MBG), and business angels Christophe Barriolade, Aldrich Huang, Jens Kosche, and Marc Scheidegger, alongside a Business Angel Bonus from Sächsische Aufbaubank. Founded in 2025 by Leon Rauch, Moritz Scherer, and Benjamín Cádiz de Gracia, the company operates out of the SpinLab accelerator in Leipzig. JawBuddy offers a smartphone application that delivers guided, physiotherapist-designed exercise routines for people experiencing jaw pain, bruxism (teeth grinding or clenching), and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) related tension. The app is registered as a Class I medical device under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and is positioned as a complement to conventional dental care. According to the company, clinical pilot projects are underway at five sites, including University Hospital RWTH Aachen. A multicentre randomised controlled trial (RCT) with 130 patients is scheduled to begin in December 2026, and JawBuddy reports it is negotiating a care contract with a major German statutory health insurer targeting a start date in early 2027.

## Key details

The funding will be used to finance the company’s own efficacy study and to advance reimbursement discussions with health insurers, CEO Leon Rauch said in the announcement. The clinical content is developed by co-founder Moritz Scherer, a physiotherapist who holds an M.Sc. and is a PhD candidate in Health Technologies, together with Dr. Christian Wolf, a practicing oral and maxillofacial surgeon at Kantonsspital Aarau in Switzerland. The company states that all exercises are evidence-based and combine clinical expertise with current research on jaw disorders. The application guides users through a personalised self-therapy programme at home and uses the smartphone camera to measure progress. Daily assessments, feedback, and symptom tracking feed an adaptive algorithm that adjusts the exercise plan over time. The app also generates exportable medical reports that patients can share with their dentist, physician, or physiotherapist to support ongoing treatment. HALBZEIT’s Pool Captain Luisa Wasilewski said the firm invests where a large underserved market, a clear clinical need, and a reimbursable model converge, and that JawBuddy addresses a problem familiar to every dental practice: patients with jaw problems who return repeatedly without resolution. The involvement of dental and maxillofacial specialists as both investors and clinical advisors signals domain validation. MBG’s participation reflects regional economic development interest in Saxony’s health technology ecosystem.

## Why it matters

JawBuddy operates at the intersection of several trends in European digital health: condition-specific self-management tools, clinical validation as a prerequisite for reimbursement, and integration with existing care pathways rather than replacement of them. Temporomandibular disorders and bruxism affect a substantial portion of the adult population, yet non-invasive, conservative management options between dental visits are limited. By registering as a Class I medical device under EU MDR, the company has cleared a baseline regulatory hurdle; the planned RCT and care contract negotiation indicate a deliberate pursuit of the German Digital Health Applications (DiGA) fast-track reimbursement pathway, which requires positive care effects demonstrated in a comparative study. Success would allow physicians and psychotherapists to prescribe the app at health-insurer expense, creating a scalable revenue model. The investor syndicate blends strategic clinical expertise (Marquardt, Sigron, Wolf), regional public funding (MBG, Sächsische Aufbaubank), and a specialised healthcare platform (HALBZEIT), suggesting the round was structured to de-risk both clinical and market-access milestones. For a product team at a bank, the case illustrates how early-stage health technology ventures in Europe increasingly align financing tranches with regulatory and reimbursement milestones, and how clinical credibility — evidenced by specialist co-development, hospital pilot sites, and a registered medical device — functions as a primary asset class in lieu of traditional revenue traction. The December 2026 RCT start and early-2027 insurer contract target are concrete near-term catalysts to monitor for evidence of execution against the stated roadmap.

climate_energy.headline: Data centers turn to jet engines amid power shortages
climate_energy.teaser: Builders are using discarded jet engines to power data centers due to grid delays.
climate_energy.whatItIs: Use of jet engines as temporary, less efficient power sources.
climate_energy.whyItMatters: Highlights the extreme measures taken to meet the massive power demands of AI.
climate_energy.bankAngle: Represents a potential ESG risk for banks financing data center infrastructure.
climate_energy.imageAlt: Data centers turn to jet engines amid power shortages

signalScore.rationale: Significant infrastructure trend with ESG implications.

climate_energy.longSummary:
## The story

AI data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows. The New York Times reported Tuesday that some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, according to TechCrunch. The engines are pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas. They are not anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant, but they are another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout.

For companies stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times that "It’s all about getting power as fast as possible." With jet-powered units, he said, "they can have a data center running in 24 months." Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years, according to the International Energy Agency.

The article describes this as a response to a growing bottleneck. As AI demand increases, some data center operators are seeking faster power options. The converted jet engines are not presented as a permanent solution, but they are being used as a temporary way to address delays in grid connections and new generation capacity. The engines are not a permanent power plant, and the article does not present them as such.

## Key details

The engines are pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas. ProEnergy rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. In 2025, OpenAI used gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April.

Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines.

Converted jet engines come with trade-offs. They are less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and they take more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play, with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two.

Most power capacity is expected to come online by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg. In some cases, delays are already costing data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it could not deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.

## Why it matters

The move matters because AI data center demand is pushing developers into unusual power sources while traditional grid access remains slow. The converted jet engines are temporary and less efficient, but they can get a data center running faster than waiting for traditional grid connections or new turbines.

The story also notes that the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity. For the climate and energy sector, the approach raises questions about efficiency and emissions. For data center builders, it may be a stopgap measure while they wait for grid capacity.

For anyone outside AI, the broader point is that the power shortage is becoming a central constraint on technology development. The jet engine example is presented as an extreme measure, but it reflects a larger gap between the pace of AI investment and the pace of new power generation. The article suggests that the wait for power is still long, and that temporary fixes may be needed while the grid catches up.

consumer_retail.whatItIs: Alcoholic versions of the viral 'dirty soda' trend.
consumer_retail.whyItMatters: Shows how restaurant chains capitalize on viral social media trends.
